overview: This is modern Benin, formerly the French colony and independent Republic of Dahomey. It is geographically and historically distinct from the Edo kingdom of Benin in Nigeria. The map begins during colonial rule; independence came in 1960 and the country adopted the name Benin in 1975.

periods.title: Late colonial Dahomey
periods.summary: The territory remained under French rule until independence on 1 August 1960.

periods.title: Independence, coups and the People’s Republic
periods.summary: Political instability was followed by military rule from 1972 and the 1975 renaming as the People’s Republic of Benin.

periods.title: National Conference and constitutional change
periods.summary: A National Conference in 1990 opened a new constitutional phase; the country continues beyond these changes of regime.

items.text: The French colony created in 1894 included territories with different earlier histories. Its name Dahomey came from the kingdom centred on Abomey, but the colonial territory was not simply that older kingdom continuing unchanged.

Independence arrived on 1 August 1960 under the name Dahomey. The country’s archives distinguish an early independence period from the military and revolutionary phase that began with the October 1972 takeover.
In 1975 the government renamed the country the People’s Republic of Benin. A National Conference in February 1990 and a new constitution that December marked another major political transition.

In north-western Benin and neighbouring Togo, Batammariba builders make earthen tower-houses called sikien; one is a takienta. A family dwelling is also connected to ancestors and ritual, so its layout has meanings beyond keeping out rain.

In these houses, animals have space on the ground floor and granaries stand on the terrace. Storage, livestock and family life occupy different parts of a carefully organized building. This describes Batammariba architecture, not every Beninese home.

Earthen houses require maintenance and rebuilding. UNESCO describes a continuing cycle of construction, abandonment and renewal, sometimes alongside newer rectangular houses with metal roofs. A living tradition can change its materials while retaining important social meanings.

Gelede performances among Yoruba-Nago communities honour the primordial mother Iyà Nlà and women’s social roles. They may follow harvests or mark important events; the tradition extends across Benin, Nigeria and Togo.

A Gelede performance needs much preparation: carvers make masks, makers assemble costumes, and singers and drummers perform before the dancers. Learning a public tradition involves many practical skills behind the scenes.

Gelede poetry can use irony and mockery, with satirical masks supporting the words. Serious community reflection and humour can share a performance; historical societies did not spend every ceremony being solemn.

In the lower Ouémé valley, Tofin and Ouémè communities maintain villages with houses on stilts. Benin’s 2020 heritage submission connects these settlements to refuge from earlier slave raids and to livelihoods adapted to water.

Seasonal flooding reshapes work on the valley’s partly submerged islands. The nomination describes roughly four flood months, followed by months when exposed land permits farming alongside fishing. A landscape can have a wet-season and a dry-season timetable.

sections.title: A small sample of official writing

items.text: The 1990 constitution gives the French motto “Fraternité-Justice-Travail”: “Fraternity, Justice, Work”. This is an attested official-language sample, not a claim that French is everyone’s home language. The same article pictures a Somba tower-house in the national arms, connecting state symbols with a regional building tradition.

ending.text: Benin continues as a country. Colonial rule ended in 1960; subsequent changes of name, ideology and constitution transformed government without ending its diverse communities.
